title: Senate impeach court set to take short break
summary: The Senate impeachment court will go on a brief hiatus this week, with trial sessions set to resume on Dec. 1, as the tribunal targets a final judgment before Congress adjourns on Dec. 18.

blocks.text: November 22, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The Senate impeachment court will go on a brief hiatus this week, with trial sessions set to resume on Dec. 1, as the tribunal targets a final judgment before Congress adjourns on Dec. 18.

Under the updated schedule, the court canceled its Nov. 26-27 hearings after lead defense counsel Sheila Sison manifested that the remaining eight to 10 defense witnesses are unavailable due to prior commitments.

Impeachment court spokesman Reginald Tongol said exhibit marking and the submission of the defense’s sequential witness list will still proceed during the week, while the Senate will hold plenary voting on the national budget on Nov. 28.
Hearings from Dec. 1 to 4 are earmarked to wrap up the defense’s presentation of evidence, followed by the formal offer of evidence from Dec. 9 to 11.
“Barring rebuttal or sur-rebuttal extensions,” the court aims to hold oral arguments and its final roll-call vote on Dec. 14 and Dec. 16 to 18.
Enough time
The targeted remaining three weeks in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte would be enough time for her defense team to present its last five to six witnesses.
Defense spokesman Michael Poa said the given time frame would be enough for Duterte’s legal team to complete its presentation of evidence.
“We were already able to take up three (witnesses) this week and then we dispensed with one. So, we’re down to around five or six,” Poa said.

“Of course, I would be a little biased by saying, yes, (the testimony of the remaining witness) will be impactful. So, definitely in our minds, in our perspective, it will be impactful because we want to end strong,” he added.
Tight schedule

Speaking to dzMM and dwIZ yesterday, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said he is looking at a very “tight” schedule in December for the ongoing impeachment proceedings, with the defense set to present their last witness and make their formal offer of evidence, and for the prosecution to respond or rebut.

Asked if there are enough days in December for the formal offer and their verdict writing break, Gatchalian said some senator-judges, like himself, have started making their analysis of the evidence presented so far to save on time.

“Of course, it’s not over yet. More evidence is still coming in. We have also begun discussing amongst ourselves. What’s important is the explanation of votes – to clarify to the public the reasons behind our vote,” he said.

Gatchalian said it was still his “personal” preference for the whole trial to end with a verdict before Christmas or New Year’s. But he admitted that the court has to be “flexible” as it cannot predict what will happen in December, with the defense set to present their last set of witnesses from Dec. 1 to 4.
He said one of the lessons of the impeachment court is to be flexible.
“We have an idea in terms of the number of days, but we remain flexible to ensure the trial runs efficiently,” Gatchalian said.

He said the before Christmas verdict date is a “moving target” similar to the Senate’s target date for passing and ratifying the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027, and in confirming the Cabinet secretaries, foreign service and military officers whose appointments and nominations have to be confirmed before Dec. 17 or the session adjournment lest they be bypassed.
Twelve Cabinet secretaries are in line for confirmation before the Commission on Appointments (CA) after having served in acting capacity for over a year.

Gatchalian said their legislative duties in the budget and CA are equally important, with the budget being “time-bound” that requires being passed before year-end, and the confirmation process is needed to end the practice of having officials in an acting capacity.
He said all these “important activities” – impeachment, budget plenary deliberations and confirmation process – “are being done by the Senate simultaneously.” — Bella Cariaso, Marc Jayson Cayabyab
